newsitem.title: CANADA: Westcoast, producers agree incentive tolls.
newsitem.headline: Westcoast, producers agree incentive tolls.

text.p: Gas pipeline company Westcoast Energy Inc said Wednesday it reached a deal with the Canadian Canadian Association of Petroleum Producers on an incentive-based toll structure for the its pipeline and field services divisions through 2001.
The announcement signalled the resolution of a longstanding dispute with producers over tolls at Westcoast's pipelines.
Westcoast said the plan was subject to approval by the National Energy Board.

A Westcoast spokeswoman stressed the accord represented only an agreement in principle and further details must be worked out before a final deal is concluded. Wescoast did not specify the issues that remained outstanding.

The new rate structure would be sensitive to gas prices in calculating gathering and processing costs, Westcoast said. The structure for transmission tolls would contain incentives under which Westcoast and its customers would share savings if Westcoast beat agreed-upon cost targets. Westcoast said it was discussing the proposal with downstream customers including BC Gas Inc, forestry companies and some U.S. utilities.

If the pipeline company reaches a final agreement with producers on the rate structure, Westcoast said it plans to drop a previous application to the National Energy Board that sought a roughly 25 percent increase in average tolls. That was based on traditional rate-setting methods.
Instead, the company would present the new arrangement to the agency at upcoming hearings.
Westcoast chairman Michael Phelps said the new structure would help create a "positive exploration and production climate in northeast British Columbia over the next five years."

"This innovative deal is a timely response to the desires of many of our customers to see a more flexible and new form of regulation for the natural gas transportation infrastructure in B.C.," he said.

Shippers had in the past raised concerns about Westcoast potentially having too great a market share in northeastern British Columbia for an alternative, flexible rate-setting system to be successful.
The Westcoast plan is similar to arrangements established by other major Canadian oil and gas pipelines over the past two years.
